title: Deep-Sea Giants
objective: After this level you can explain why some deep-sea animals grow so large.
summary: Many deep animals outgrow their shallow relatives. Cold slows their lives, few predators trouble them, and big bodies cope better when food is scarce.

cards.headline: The pill bug in your garden has a deep-sea cousin longer than a school ruler.
cards.body: Giant isopods crawl the deep sea floor and can grow more than 30 cm long. They aren't alone: down in the cold and dark, animal after animal comes in an oversized edition. Why does the deep grow giants?

cards.headline: Supersized
cards.body: Giant isopods are much larger than their shallow-water relatives, and so are many other deep-sea animals. Scientists call it deep-sea gigantism. Remember Level 54's colossal squid, the heaviest invertebrate on Earth? It's one of the pattern's headliners.

cards.headline: Slow and steady
cards.body: Scientists aren't sure what drives it, and several causes may work together. One is the cold: chilly deep water slows animals' metabolisms, and many deep-sea creatures grow and mature very slowly. Another is that few predators bother a big, armored isopod, so it can take its time. Growing up slowly, it turns out, can mean growing up big.

cards.headline: A body built for lean times
cards.body: Food is scarce down here, and a big body helps. Larger animals can travel farther to find food, use energy more efficiently and store more of it. One giant isopod in a Japanese aquarium reportedly went about five years without eating. Size is the deep sea's packed lunch.

mascot.line: Five years without a snack. I get grumpy after five hours.

cards.headline: Deep-sea giants: sized up
learned: Many deep animals outgrow their shallow relatives
Few predators give time to grow
Big bodies travel farther and store more food

questions.prompt: What do scientists mean by deep-sea gigantism?

options.label: Deep-sea animals living longer than land animals
Giant waves in the deep ocean
Deep-sea animals growing larger than their shallow relatives

questions.explanation: Many deep-sea animals, like giant isopods, grow much larger than their shallow-water relatives.

questions.prompt: How can a bigger body help an animal survive where food is scarce?

options.label: It can travel farther and store more energy
It stays warmer than the water around it
options.rationale: The reasons given are travel, efficiency and storage.

options.label: It scares away every predator in the area
options.rationale: That's not how size helps with scarce food.

options.label: It lets the animal make its own food
options.rationale: Size doesn't let an animal make food.

questions.explanation: Larger animals can travel farther to find food, use energy more efficiently and store more of it.

questions.prompt: Level 51's midnight zone stays at a steady 4°C. How might that cold help deep-sea animals grow large?

options.label: Cold water is thicker and holds animals up
Cold water kills off all their predators
options.rationale: It's about how their bodies run.

options.label: Cold water makes food far more plentiful
Cold slows metabolism, so they grow slowly

questions.explanation: Cold slows metabolism; many deep-sea animals grow and mature slowly, which may help them reach large sizes.
